locations.name: Sacré-Cœur and Square Louise-Michel
locations.identify: The white basilica with its domes crowns the hill; below it, Square Louise-Michel climbs in curving paths, terraces and staircases. Start at the bottom, on Place Saint-Pierre, by the carousel, and look up.

access.wheelchair: via the funicular from Place Saint-Pierre to the top
access.notes: Climbing the square takes about ten minutes; the funicular uses a Métro ticket.

facts.text: The treasure-hunt sequence starts on the lowest tier of Square Louise-Michel, looking up at the basilica; Nino follows painted arrows along the curving paths and climbs the steps on the right of the square.
Amélie phones Nino from a public phone near the carousel in Place Saint-Pierre; the phone is no longer there, and it was possibly a prop.
At the Vue de Paris viewpoint, a statue performer points Nino towards a telescope; the telescope on the next tier has since been removed.
Amélie arranges for Nino to meet her at the base of the steps, then sets up a treasure hunt that ends at the basilica; a vintage carousel turns at the foot of the steps.

The basilica of the Sacré-Cœur (Wikidata Q28785) was begun in 1875 to designs by Paul Abadie, in a Romanesque and Byzantine Revival style; it is a protected historic monument (Mérimée PA75180004). Square Louise-Michel (Q3494691) dates from 1877.

scenes.description: To return Nino's lost photo album without revealing herself, Amélie lays a trail for him: painted arrows lead him up through Square Louise-Michel, she calls him at a public phone near the carousel, and a statue performer at the Vue de Paris viewpoint points him to a telescope.

texts.html: Up there is the Sacré-Cœur, the white church on top of Montmartre. In the film, Amélie sends Nino on a treasure hunt through this garden, with painted arrows on the paths. Follow them up! Nino is the shy young man Amélie falls in love with. The telescope Nino looks through has been removed.

This is the big moment of the film. Amélie has found Nino's lost photo album, but she is too shy to just give it back. So she invents a treasure hunt! Painted arrows lead Nino up the paths of this garden, Square Louise-Michel, towards the white domes of the Sacré-Cœur. Amélie is a French film from 2001. Amélie is a shy young woman, and Nino is the young man who collects lost photos and makes her heart beat faster. Did you know? The telescope Nino looks through at the viewpoint has been removed, and the phone Amélie calls him on was probably a prop.

Along the way, Amélie phones him from a public phone near the carousel at the bottom, and a man pretending to be a statue points Nino towards a telescope at the viewpoint. Everything is planned like a game.

Climb the paths yourself and stop at the viewpoint near the top. Turn around: all of Paris is below you.

Tip: start at the old carousel at the bottom, then follow the curving paths and the steps on the right side of the garden, just like Nino.

Look up! On the very top of the hill of Montmartre stands the Sacré-Cœur, a white basilica with round domes that you can see from all over Paris. Building it began in 1875, and it took many years to finish. Below it, a garden called Square Louise-Michel climbs the hill with curving paths, terraces and staircases. In the film Amélie, this garden is the stage for a great treasure hunt. Amélie is a French film from 2001 about Amélie Poulain, a shy young woman who secretly helps people. Nino is the young man she falls for: he collects lost photos from photo booths. Detectives, take note: the telescope from the film has been removed, and the public phone near the carousel was probably a prop that the film crew brought with them.

Here is the story. Nino has lost his precious photo album, and Amélie has found it. But she is too shy to simply hand it back. Instead, she leads him on a treasure hunt! Painted arrows on the paths guide Nino up the garden. At the bottom, near the carousel, Amélie calls him on a public telephone. Higher up, at the viewpoint, a man dressed as a statue points to a telescope, and through the telescope Nino finds the next clue. Amélie watches everything from her hiding place.

Start your own treasure hunt at the bottom, on Place Saint-Pierre, next to the old carousel. Then climb the paths and the steps on the right side of the square, like Nino does. When you reach the viewpoint, stop and turn around: the whole city of Paris is spread out below you.

If your legs are tired, there is a little funicular railway that climbs the hill next to the garden, and it uses a Métro ticket.

Group game: in teams, invent a mini treasure hunt for another team with three clues hidden in what you can see from the viewpoint. Use only words and pointing, no drawing on anything!

One more secret: the film makes its colours warmer and more golden than real life. Look at the white stone of the basilica and compare it with your memory of the film. Which version of Paris do you prefer, the real one or the film one?

The setting of Amélie's treasure hunt: painted arrows lead Nino up Square Louise-Michel towards the basilica, guided by phone calls and a statue performer. The telescope and the phone have gone; the paths remain. Amélie returns Nino's lost album this way, too shy to do it face to face. Start on the lowest tier, the sequence's opening view.

The Sacré-Cœur basilica, begun in 1875 to designs by Paul Abadie, crowns the Butte Montmartre; the garden below it, Square Louise-Michel, laid out in 1877, descends in terraces, curving paths and staircases to Place Saint-Pierre. In Amélie, the garden becomes a giant game board. Too shy to return Nino's lost photo album in person, Amélie lays a trail of painted arrows up the paths, calls him from a public phone near the carousel, and stations a statue performer at the viewpoint to point him to a telescope. Amélie (2001), by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, is the story of a shy Montmartre waitress who arranges other people's happiness while avoiding her own. A comparison made for the film's anniversary notes that the payphone was possibly a prop, that its spot is now a concrete area, and that the telescope on the upper tier has been removed.

Begin on the lowest tier, which gives the sequence's first view of the basilica, then climb the right-hand steps as Nino does. The funicular is the easy way up.

Arrive early in the morning to have the paths, and the view from the top terrace, almost to yourself.

The Sacré-Cœur is the great white signature of the Paris skyline. Begun in 1875 to designs by Paul Abadie, in a Romanesque and Byzantine Revival style that set it apart from the city's Gothic and classical churches, the basilica sits on the summit of the Butte Montmartre and is now a protected historic monument. Below it, Square Louise-Michel, laid out in 1877, falls away in terraces, curving paths and staircases to Place Saint-Pierre and its carousel. Amélie (Le Fabuleux Destin d'Amélie Poulain, 2001), by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, follows a solitary waitress who quietly improves other people's lives. Its romance with Nino, a collector of discarded photo-booth portraits, plays out as an elaborate game of hide-and-seek. The sequence turns the monument into a backdrop for play rather than devotion: the camera keeps the basilica in the upper frame as a goal, while the action happens on the garden's winding paths.

In the film, the square stages the climax of that game. Amélie has found the album Nino lost and decides to return it without revealing herself. She lays a trail of painted arrows that lead him up the curving paths; she rings him from a public phone near the carousel at the bottom; and at the Vue de Paris viewpoint a statue performer points him to a telescope, through which he finds the next clue. Amélie, hidden, directs the whole operation.

The British Film Institute's anniversary comparison followed the sequence on the ground. The lowest tier of the square gives the opening view of the basilica; Nino climbs the steps on the right of the square; the stonework of a fountain near the top is still recognisable. Some props have gone: the payphone, possibly brought in by the crew, has left a patch of concrete, and the telescope on the upper tier has been removed.

To follow the hunt, start by the carousel on Place Saint-Pierre and climb on foot; the funicular alongside is the gentle alternative. The top terrace offers one of the great views over Paris, best in the early morning before the crowds, or at sunset, when the stone of the basilica turns pink and gold, like a frame from the film.

Allow at least forty minutes for the climb, the terrace and the view.

A monument recast as a game board: in Amélie, the basilica is a goal at the top of the frame while the romance plays out on the garden paths below. The square stages the treasure hunt that returns Nino's album. Several props, the payphone and the telescope, have since gone.

The treasure-hunt sequence of Amélie (2001) uses Square Louise-Michel, laid out in 1877 below the basilica of the Sacré-Cœur (begun 1875, Paul Abadie), as a ludic space. Arrows painted on the paths, a payphone call and a statue performer's gesture choreograph Nino's ascent, while Amélie directs the encounter from concealment. The monument is subordinated to play: it marks the goal at the top of the frame rather than the meaning of the scene. A ludic space is one organised as a game, with rules, clues and a goal. The British Film Institute's location comparison records the impermanence of the set dressing: the payphone was possibly a prop, its spot is now concrete, and the telescope on the upper tier has been removed.

The site thus shows both continuity, in the paths, steps and fountain stonework, and loss, in the props that made the scene legible.

Comparing the permanent garden with the vanished props is a compact way to discuss what visitors to a film location actually come to verify: the architecture, or the scene.

The Sacré-Cœur, begun in 1875 to designs by Paul Abadie and protected as a historic monument, is among the most reproduced images of Paris. Amélie (2001) uses it in an unexpected way. In the film's treasure-hunt sequence, the basilica functions as a destination fixed at the top of the frame, while the meaning of the scene lies in the garden below, Square Louise-Michel, laid out in 1877, whose terraces and curving paths become a board for a game. In Jean-Pierre Jeunet's film, the shy heroine returns a lost photo album to Nino through an elaborate, anonymous game rather than a face-to-face meeting. The sequence can be read as a miniature of the film's method: the city is used not as heritage but as a playful, legible space, and its most famous monument is reduced to a landmark that orients the action.

The game is carefully choreographed. Painted arrows lead Nino up the paths; Amélie calls him from a public phone near the carousel on Place Saint-Pierre; and at the Vue de Paris viewpoint a statue performer gestures towards a telescope, which reveals the next clue. Amélie remains concealed throughout, which extends the film's pattern of benevolent control: she can give, but not yet be seen giving.

The site's afterlife is documented in the British Film Institute's anniversary comparison, which traced the sequence tier by tier. The lowest tier still gives the opening view of the basilica; Nino's route up the right-hand steps and the stonework of a fountain near the top remain recognisable. The props have not survived: the payphone, possibly brought in by the production, has left only a concrete patch, and the telescope on the upper tier has been removed. A visitor following the scene therefore reconstructs it from the permanent architecture of the garden, while the devices that carried the plot exist only on film.

This combination of persistent structure and vanished props is typical of location tourism, and it makes the square a good place to discuss what exactly fans come to verify.

In this sense the square invites a reflection on authenticity: the garden is genuine, but the experience fans seek here was produced by objects that existed only for the duration of the shoot.

locations.name: Métro Abbesses
locations.identify: In the middle of Place des Abbesses: a glass canopy shaped like a fan on green cast-iron stems, with the word “Métropolitain” in curling Art Nouveau letters. A carousel often turns beside it.

access.notes: The platforms are 36 metres down: take the lift, or the long spiral staircase if you are feeling fit.

facts.text: One guide places Amélie's first encounter with Nino at Abbesses station.
The scenes inside the station were not filmed at Abbesses but at Porte des Lilas, a disused “ghost” station that served as a set.
Abbesses station lies 36 metres underground and is served by two lifts and two spiral staircases.
The entrance on Place des Abbesses is one of Hector Guimard's Art Nouveau Métro canopies, with a glass roof and the word “Métropolitain”.

texts.html: In the film, this Métro station is where Amélie first sees Nino, a strange young man who collects torn-up photos from photo booths. Look at the beautiful green and glass entrance! Amélie is a 2001 French film about a shy girl who secretly helps people. Secret: the scenes inside were filmed at another, closed station!

Look at this entrance: a glass roof shaped like a fan, green iron stems that look like plants, and curly letters spelling “Métropolitain”. It was designed in the Art Nouveau style by Hector Guimard, who drew many of the old Métro entrances of Paris. Amélie is a French film from 2001 about Amélie Poulain, a shy young woman who decides to make other people happy in secret. Film secret: the scenes inside the station were not filmed here at all, but at Porte des Lilas, a closed “ghost” station that film crews use as a set.

In the story, this is the station where Amélie first notices Nino. He is on his knees beside a photo booth, collecting the little photos people tore up and threw away. Why would anyone collect them? You will find out on the tour!

Fun fact: the platforms are 36 metres underground, so deep that there are two lifts and two spiral staircases. Count the steps if you dare!

Before you go down, look closely at the green iron stems: can you see how they curl like plant stalks?

Welcome to Place des Abbesses, one of the prettiest squares in Montmartre, and to one of the most beautiful Métro entrances in the world. Look up: a glass roof shaped like a fan, held up by green iron stems that curl like plants, and above the stairs the word “Métropolitain” in swirly letters. This style is called Art Nouveau, and the entrance was designed by Hector Guimard, who drew many of the old Métro entrances of Paris around the year 1900. Amélie is a French film from 2001. Its heroine, Amélie Poulain, is a shy young woman with a huge imagination who decides to help the people around her in secret. Here is the twist: the scenes inside the station were not filmed at Abbesses at all. They were shot at Porte des Lilas, a closed “ghost” station that is only used by film crews.

In the story, this station is where Amélie first notices Nino. He is a young man who does something very strange: he crawls around photo booths and collects the little photos that people tore up and threw away. Then he glues them back together in a big album. Amélie is curious, and from that moment the two of them start a long game of hide-and-seek all over Paris.

Abbesses is also a record breaker. Its platforms lie 36 metres underground, much deeper than most stations, so there are two lifts and two spiral staircases. Walking down the long spiral staircase feels like going deep into the hill itself.

While you are in the square, look around: there is often a carousel turning next to the entrance, and the cafés around the square are full of people watching the world go by, just like Amélie loves to do.

Mini challenge: Nino collects other people's lost photos. Imagine you found one torn photo on the floor today. Who might be in it, and why was it torn? Invent the story in three sentences.

Look carefully at the entrance before you leave. The iron is shaped like plants: stalks, leaves and buds. The glass roof spreads out like a fan or a shell. Guimard wanted the Métro to feel natural and magical, not just practical. Do you think he succeeded? Which plant does it remind you of?

The station of Amélie's first encounter with Nino, the young man who rescues discarded photo-booth pictures. Above ground, one of Hector Guimard's glass-roofed Art Nouveau entrances. Amélie (2001) follows a shy waitress who secretly arranges small happinesses for others. The interiors were actually shot at Porte des Lilas, a disused station.

Place des Abbesses is the gateway to upper Montmartre, and its Métro entrance is one of the best-preserved examples of Hector Guimard's Art Nouveau designs: a glass canopy fanned out on green cast-iron stems, crowned by the word “Métropolitain”. In the story of Amélie, the station is where the heroine first notices Nino, a young man who collects torn-up photographs abandoned around photo booths and pieces them back together in an album. Amélie (2001), directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, follows a solitary Montmartre waitress who decides to improve other people's lives anonymously. As so often, the story's geography and the shooting geography part ways here: the platform scenes were filmed at Porte des Lilas, a disused “ghost” station kept for film crews.

The station itself is remarkable: its platforms lie 36 metres below the square, served by two lifts and two spiral staircases decorated with murals. Take the lift down and the stairs up only if you enjoy a climb.

Look at the cast-iron stems closely: Guimard modelled them on plant forms, a hallmark of Art Nouveau design.

Place des Abbesses, with its plane trees, cafés and carousel, is where many visitors first meet upper Montmartre. At its centre stands one of Hector Guimard's celebrated Métro entrances: a glass canopy fanned out on green cast-iron stems, with the word “Métropolitain” in sinuous Art Nouveau lettering. Guimard's entrances, designed around 1900 for the young Métro, have become emblems of Paris in their own right. Amélie (Le Fabuleux Destin d'Amélie Poulain, 2001), directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, follows Amélie Poulain, a shy waitress who decides to bring happiness to the people around her without being noticed. Behind the scenes, the station sequences were filmed not at Abbesses but at Porte des Lilas, a disused “ghost” station that the network keeps for filming, a common practice that spares a busy line from a film crew.

In the story, Abbesses is where Amélie first notices Nino Quincampoix. He is an odd figure: he collects the torn-up photographs that people throw away around photo booths and reassembles them in a scrapbook. Among his finds, one face keeps returning, a mysterious man who seems to leave his picture in booths all over Paris. Nino's album, and the chase it sets off, drive the romantic half of the film.

The station is also one of the deepest in the network: its platforms lie 36 metres underground, reached by two lifts and two spiral staircases. Walking down feels like descending into the hill, and it is worth doing once, if only to understand why most people queue for the lift.

Up in the square, the Guimard canopy is the obvious photograph, best taken from the southern side with the trees behind it. On a quiet morning, with the carousel still covered and the cafés setting out their chairs, the square has the slightly theatrical calm that Jeunet's film gives to the whole neighbourhood.

Practical note: the square is most photogenic early in the day, before the café terraces fill. Line 12 brings you straight here from the centre; the climb from the platforms by the spiral stairs is long, so use the lifts unless you want the full experience. From the square, Rue des Abbesses leads west towards Rue Lepic and the Café des 2 Moulins, while the streets to the east climb towards the Sacré-Cœur, which makes Abbesses a natural starting point for an Amélie walk.

The diegetic station of Amélie's first sight of Nino; the interiors were shot at Porte des Lilas, a disused station. A clear case of a story location and a filming location parting ways. Diegetic means within the story world. The Guimard canopy keeps the place recognisable regardless.

Abbesses illustrates the distinction between setting and location. In Amélie's story world, the station is where the heroine first notices Nino, the collector of discarded photo-booth portraits; the interior scenes, however, were filmed at Porte des Lilas, a disused station used as a set. The recognisable element that ties the fiction to the real square is architectural: one of Hector Guimard's Art Nouveau entrances, with its glass canopy and “Métropolitain” lettering. Setting is where a story says it happens; location is where it was actually filmed. The two often differ for practical reasons. Nino's practice of reassembling strangers' torn portraits is one of the film's self-reflexive motifs: an amateur archive of anonymous images, assembled much as a film is assembled from fragments.

The station's depth, 36 metres below the square, reached by lifts and spiral stairs, makes it a memorable descent into the hill of Montmartre.

For an itinerary, Abbesses therefore works best as a threshold: the point where the visitor enters the film's Montmartre, rather than a place where its images can be checked against reality.

Abbesses is a textbook case of the gap between a story's setting and a film's locations. Within the fiction of Amélie, the station is where the heroine first notices Nino Quincampoix, the young man who collects photographs torn up and abandoned around photo booths. The platform scenes were nevertheless filmed at Porte des Lilas, a disused “ghost” station used as a set. The place a visitor can verify is therefore the entrance and the square, not the interiors seen on screen. Amélie (2001), directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet and co-written with Guillaume Laurant, is set almost entirely in a small part of the 18th arrondissement, which makes its few departures from real geography all the more instructive. Ghost stations are a practical resource of urban film-making: they offer authentic Métro architecture without disrupting a working line, but they detach the image from the named place, which is precisely what location tourism tries to reattach.

Nino's hobby is among the film's richest motifs. His album of reassembled strangers is an archive of the anonymous, and its recurring mystery man, whose portrait appears in booths across the city, becomes the engine of the romance. The motif is self-reflexive: a collection of fragments, cut and glued into a sequence, is not far from a description of editing itself. That the scenes evoking it were assembled in another station only reinforces the point.

The square supplies the architectural anchor that the interiors cannot. Its entrance is one of Hector Guimard's Art Nouveau designs for the early Métro, a glass canopy fanned on cast-iron stems and topped by sinuous “Métropolitain” lettering. Guimard's entrances, once controversial, are now among the most reproduced images of Paris, and their presence here allows the station to function as a recognisable stop on any Amélie itinerary.

The station's depth, some 36 metres below the square and reached by lifts and two spiral staircases, adds a further layer: a vertical journey into the hill that the film's interiors, filmed elsewhere, cannot share.

For an itinerary built around the film, Abbesses works best as a threshold rather than a site of verification: it introduces the visitor to the film's Montmartre and to its central mechanism, the collection and reassembly of fragments, while openly showing that the images themselves were made somewhere else.

locations.name: Métro Lamarck – Caulaincourt
locations.identify: A Métro station built into the steep north slope of Montmartre, between Rue Caulaincourt below and Rue Lamarck above; look for the Métro sign and the flights of steps that climb beside the entrance towards Rue de la Fontaine-du-But.

access.notes: The steps are steep; the station is an ordinary, busy stop, so keep the stairs clear.

On screen the shops seem to sit right beside the station exit; in reality they are nearby, not next to it.
Lamarck – Caulaincourt is a station on Métro line 12, close to where Amélie lives in the film.

texts.html: Here Amélie does one of her kindest deeds. She takes a blind man by the arm and describes everything she sees on the way, then leaves him at this Métro station and runs up the steps. Amélie is a 2001 film about a shy girl who secretly helps people. Which staircase did she run up? The one on the right!

This is one of the sweetest scenes of the whole film. Amélie sees a blind man waiting to cross the street. She takes his arm and walks him along Rue Lamarck very fast, describing everything around them: the shop windows, the smells, a dog, a baby, the people. Then, at this Métro station, she leaves him and runs away up the steps, and the man stands there smiling, full of pictures. Amélie is a French film from 2001. Its heroine is a shy young woman who decides to help the people around her in secret. Small detail: on screen the shops look as if they are right next to the station, but in real life they are a little further along the street.

Try it yourself, carefully and with a partner: close your eyes while your partner describes the street to you for one minute. Then swap. What did you notice that you would never have seen with your eyes open? Stay on the pavement, away from the steps and the road.

Welcome to Lamarck – Caulaincourt, a Métro station tucked into the steep north side of the hill of Montmartre. It has a long name because it sits between two streets, Rue Lamarck up the hill and Rue Caulaincourt down below, and it is a stop on line 12. For film fans, it is the place where Amélie does one of her kindest good deeds. Amélie is a French film from 2001. Amélie Poulain is a shy young woman who decides, one day, to make other people happier without them knowing it was her. If you have seen the film, you will remember how fast this scene goes: the camera races along with Amélie, and the words pour out of her almost faster than you can read the subtitles.

In the film, Amélie sees a blind man standing at the edge of the pavement. Instead of just helping him across, she grabs his arm and takes him on a tour of the street, describing everything: the shop windows, what people are buying, a dog, a baby in a pram, the smells. She is like a radio commentator! At the Métro station she leaves him, and she runs up the staircase on the right, onto Rue de la Fontaine-du-But.

When you look around, you may notice something strange: in the film the shops seem to be right next to the station exit, but in real life they are a short walk away. Films often squeeze places together to tell a story faster. This is called editing, and you can watch out for it at every stop today.

Now a challenge for your group. Work in pairs. One person closes their eyes; the other gently guides them for ten steps, only by describing the street in words: what is in front of you, what you can hear, what you can smell. Then swap roles. Afterwards, talk about it: was it easier to guide or to be guided? What did the words help you to imagine?

Be careful on the steps: they are steep, and real passengers use them all day. If you want the film view, stand on the pavement of Rue Caulaincourt below the station and look up the slope, just like the camera.

The blind man scene: Amélie walks a stranger along Rue Lamarck in a breathless commentary on the street, then leaves him at this station and runs up the right-hand stairs. Amélie (2001) is Jean-Pierre Jeunet's comedy about a secret benefactor in Montmartre. The shops are nearby, not beside the exit as they appear.

Lamarck – Caulaincourt, on Métro line 12, sits where the north slope of Montmartre drops from Rue Lamarck to Rue Caulaincourt. In Amélie it closes one of the film's most quoted sequences. Amélie spots a blind man about to cross the street, takes his arm and, rather than simply helping, walks him at speed along Rue Lamarck while narrating everything they pass: the shop displays, a passing dog, a baby in a pram, the people on the pavement. At the station she lets go and runs up the right-hand staircase onto Rue de la Fontaine-du-But. In Amélie (2001), the title character is a young waitress who anonymously improves the lives of the people around her. The scene is a good example of the film's compression of geography: on screen the shops appear right beside the station exit, whereas in reality they are a little further along the street.

The station is a working stop, so stand clear of the steps when you look for the angle. The best view is from the pavement of Rue Caulaincourt, looking up the slope towards the stairs.

Few places show the vertical character of Montmartre as clearly as Lamarck – Caulaincourt. The station on line 12 is set into the hillside: Rue Caulaincourt passes below, Rue Lamarck runs above, and flights of steps climb beside the entrance towards Rue de la Fontaine-du-But. In Amélie, this staircase is where one of the film's best-loved sequences comes to an end. Amélie (Le Fabuleux Destin d'Amélie Poulain, 2001), by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, follows a shy waitress in Montmartre who decides to arrange small happinesses for others without being seen. The sequence is built as an accelerating montage: quick, close shots of shop windows and passers-by cut to Amélie's rapid voice, so that the audience shares the blind man's experience of a city assembled from descriptions.

Amélie notices a blind man hesitating at the kerb. Instead of the expected small kindness, she takes his arm and sweeps him along Rue Lamarck, describing everything around them in a breathless running commentary: what the shops are selling, a dog, a baby in a pram, the passers-by. At the station she lets go of him and dashes up the right-hand staircase onto Rue de la Fontaine-du-But. The man is left standing on the corner, transfigured, and the film cuts away before he can thank her.

Visitors who walk the route notice that the film has rearranged the street. On screen the shops appear right beside the station exit; in reality they are nearby, but not next to it. The compression is typical of how location filming works: separate set-ups, shot in different spots, are cut together into a single continuous walk that never existed as such.

The best way to visit is to walk a short stretch of Rue Lamarck yourself and then stop below the station, on Rue Caulaincourt, looking up at the steps. The station is a busy neighbourhood stop, so keep the stairs clear for passengers and take your photographs from the pavement. In the afternoon, the light comes round onto the slope and the cream-coloured buildings warm up, much as they do in the film's golden grade. From here, the café on Rue Lepic and the grocery on Rue des Trois Frères are both within a ten-minute walk over the hill.

The end point of the blind man sequence, where Amélie's narration of the street stops and she vanishes up the stairs. Real geography is compressed: the shops are near, not beside, the exit. Editing can join separate places into one walk. Montage here simulates perception through description.

In the blind man sequence of Amélie (2001), the protagonist walks a stranger along Rue Lamarck while improvising an exuberant verbal description of the street, then leaves him at Lamarck – Caulaincourt station and runs up the right-hand staircase onto Rue de la Fontaine-du-But. The scene condenses the film's ethic of small, unsolicited gifts and its preference for anonymity: the benefactor disappears before thanks can be given. Jean-Pierre Jeunet's film follows a young waitress in Montmartre who secretly intervenes in other people's lives. Formally, rapid cutting of shop-window details to Amélie's commentary reconstructs the city as language, a montage of descriptions offered to a man who cannot see it.

The location also shows the gap between filmed and real space: visitors note that the shops which appear right next to the station exit are in fact a short distance away. The continuous walk is an editorial construction assembled from separate set-ups, and walking the street yourself makes that construction tangible and easy to measure.

Lamarck – Caulaincourt is the terminus of one of Amélie's most frequently cited sequences, and a useful site for thinking about how location filming builds space. In the scene, Amélie takes a blind man's arm and walks him at speed along Rue Lamarck, improvising a dense description of everything they pass; at the station she releases him and runs up the right-hand staircase onto Rue de la Fontaine-du-But, leaving him transfigured on the corner. Amélie (2001), directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet and co-written with Guillaume Laurant, follows a solitary waitress who decides to improve the lives of her neighbours anonymously. The sequence can be read alongside the film's broader interest in mediated perception: photographs collected from booths, a painter copying a Renoir for decades, a voice-over that catalogues likes and dislikes. Here the medium is speech, and the city reaches the blind man as an edited sequence of verbal images.

Narratively, the episode crystallises Amélie's ethic of the gift: generous, unsolicited and anonymous. The benefactor withdraws before she can be thanked, a pattern the film repeats until its final act forces her to accept reciprocity. The blind man's moment of joy is therefore also a portrait of Amélie's avoidance of being seen.

As a location, the station illustrates spatial compression. Visitors who walk the route observe that the shops which appear right beside the station exit on screen are in fact nearby rather than adjacent. The continuous walk is a construction of editing, assembled from set-ups filmed at different points along the street. The station's own topography, set into the slope between Rue Caulaincourt and Rue Lamarck with stairs climbing towards Rue de la Fontaine-du-But, supplies the vertical exit that gives the scene its punctuation: the heroine literally rises out of the frame.

Visiting the site, one can compare the felt continuity of the scene with the measured distances on the ground, a simple exercise that makes the work of montage visible. It is worth pacing the route from the corner of Rue Lamarck to the foot of the stairs and timing it against the scene: the film's walk is shorter, faster and denser than the street itself, and the difference is a measure of how much the city on screen has been edited. The same exercise can be repeated at other stops on the tour, where the film joins places that are far apart.

texts.html: Meet the grumpy grocer Collignon! In the film, Amélie buys her fruit in this green shop, and she lives in the same building. Can you find the sign that says “Maison Collignon”? In Amélie, Collignon is mean to his kind helper Lucien, so Amélie secretly gets even. Check the side window: it is covered with newspaper stories about the film.

This little green shop is one of the most famous grocers in the world, and all because of a film. In Amélie, it belongs to Monsieur Collignon, a grumpy man who is always nasty to his young helper, Lucien. Amélie lives upstairs, in the same building, so she shops here all the time. Amélie is a French film from 2001. Its heroine, Amélie Poulain, is a shy waitress who decides to make other people happier, and sometimes to give unkind people a little lesson. Remember the rainy scene where Amélie waits with her polka-dot umbrella? From the shop door you can see the steps at the top of the Passage des Abbesses, just like in that shot.

The shop is real and still open. Look for the burgundy awning, the crates of fruit and the sign “Maison Collignon”, which was named after the film character. Inside, there is now a little crêperie too, and the window on the side is covered with newspaper articles about Amélie.

Your mission: find the first door on the west side of the building. In the film, that is the way into Amélie's flat.

Welcome to Rue des Trois Frères, the street of the three brothers, and to the most famous fruit and vegetable shop in Paris. Its real name is Au Marché de la Butte, the market of the hill, but film fans know it by another name: Collignon's grocery. Look up above the canopy and you will even see a sign that says “Maison Collignon”. In the French film Amélie, from 2001, a shy young woman called Amélie Poulain decides to secretly help the people in her neighbourhood. Some people get presents and surprises; some unkind people get a lesson. Fans call this shop Collignon's grocery, but in the film it is also the building where Amélie lives, which makes it the true centre of her little world, together with the café on Rue Lepic.

In the film, Collignon is a bully. He makes fun of his assistant Lucien, a kind and slightly clumsy young man who arranges the fruit. Amélie sees everything, and she decides that Collignon needs a lesson. So she secretly plays tricks on him in his own flat, small changes that drive him crazy, while Lucien keeps smiling in the shop. It is one of the funniest parts of the story.

There is also a quiet, rainy scene where Amélie waits outside the shop with a polka-dot umbrella. From the shop, you can look up the street and see the steps at the top of the Passage des Abbesses, just as in the film. Try to find that view.

The shop is still open. It sells fruit, vegetables and groceries, and now it has a little crêperie as well. The window on the side of the building is covered with newspaper cuttings about the film, and there is a poster too. In the film, Amélie's flat is in this building, and visitors say you reach it through the first door on the west side. Of course, real people live there, so admire the door from the street, keep your voices low and let the shoppers pass.

Discuss with your group: Amélie's tricks on Collignon are funny, but are they fair? When is it right to take revenge for someone else, and when is it better to talk to them?

Collignon's grocery from Amélie: a real corner shop below the heroine's on-screen flat. It still sells fruit and vegetables, now with a film-themed crêperie and press cuttings in the window. In the film, the bullying grocer Collignon torments his assistant Lucien until Amélie intervenes. The “Maison Collignon” sign above the canopy is a nod to the film.

On the corner of Rue des Trois Frères and Rue Androuet, this greengrocer plays Monsieur Collignon's shop in Amélie. The fictional Collignon is the neighbourhood bully, forever humiliating his gentle assistant Lucien; Amélie, who lives upstairs, answers with a campaign of secret pranks in the grocer's own flat. Amélie (2001), directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, follows a shy Montmartre waitress who anonymously rewards kindness and punishes cruelty. A rainy early sequence frames Amélie with a polka-dot umbrella while she waits to be served; the reverse view from the shop takes in the steps at the top of the Passage des Abbesses.

The real shop, Au Marché de la Butte, is still trading and has embraced its fame: a “Maison Collignon” sign hangs above the canopy, a crêperie named after the film has been added, and the west-side window is papered with press cuttings. The building is also, in the film, Amélie's home; visitors locate her door as the first one on the west side. It is a private residence, so a photograph from the pavement is the polite limit.

If the Café des 2 Moulins is where Amélie works, this corner of Rue des Trois Frères is where she lives. In the film, her flat is in this building, above the grocery of Monsieur Collignon, and the shop is one of the most frequently revisited spaces in the story. It sits on a sloping, cobbled corner of the Butte, a few minutes' walk from Place des Abbesses. Amélie (Le Fabuleux Destin d'Amélie Poulain, 2001) tells the story of a solitary young waitress who, after returning a lost box of childhood treasures to its owner, starts improving the lives of her neighbours in secret. Jeunet uses the grocery as a moral barometer: every scene there measures Collignon's cruelty against Lucien's patience, and Amélie's intervention is the film's clearest case of mischief in the service of justice.

Collignon is the neighbourhood's petty tyrant. He mocks Lucien, his assistant, in front of the customers, and he is rude to everyone he considers beneath him. Amélie decides to retaliate. She copies his keys and, over several days, makes small changes in his flat, enough to unsettle him completely, while Lucien gradually gains confidence downstairs. The sequence is played as farce, but it also shows Amélie's darker, more controlling side, a point the film never quite resolves.

The British Film Institute's comparison of locations notes that the shop is still open. It now also runs a crêperie named after the film, with a wall of press cuttings and a poster. A rainy early sequence shows Amélie waiting to be served with a polka-dot umbrella, and from the shop the steps at the top of the Passage des Abbesses are visible; standing at the door, you can still match that reverse view.

The shop front is easy to recognise: green woodwork, a burgundy awning lettered “Au Marché de la Butte”, crates of produce on the pavement and, above the wrought-iron canopy, a sign reading “Maison Collignon”, an affectionate borrowing from the fiction. Visitors also identify Amélie's front door as the first door on the west side of the building. It is a real residential entrance, so a quick photograph from across the street is the courteous way to visit, ideally on a quiet weekday morning.

A grocery that now carries its fictional name: the “Maison Collignon” sign, a film-themed crêperie and press cuttings in the window turn a working shop into an exhibit of its own screen history. In the film it is Collignon's shop, below Amélie's flat. Fiction here has been written back onto the façade.

Au Marché de la Butte is one of the two domestic anchors of Amélie's Montmartre, with the café on Rue Lepic. Narratively it combines home (Amélie's flat in the same building) and community (the shop as public stage), and it hosts the film's most sustained moral subplot: the humiliation of Lucien by the grocer Collignon and Amélie's covert retaliation. Jean-Pierre Jeunet's Amélie (2001) structures its story around a small, walkable neighbourhood in the 18th arrondissement. The pranks Amélie inflicts on Collignon have often been read as the film's most ambivalent material: playful in tone, but a portrait of benevolent surveillance and control.

The site's afterlife illustrates how film tourism can be written back onto a façade. The shop has added a “Maison Collignon” sign and a crêperie named after the film, displays press cuttings in its window, and still trades as a grocery. Fans also identify the first door on the west side of the building as Amélie's entrance, extending the fiction to a private home.

Au Marché de la Butte occupies a corner of Rue des Trois Frères that functions, in Jeunet's film, as the point where Amélie's private and public lives meet. Her flat is in the same building; the shop below is a public stage where the neighbourhood's power relations are performed daily. Together with the Café des 2 Moulins on Rue Lepic, it forms the domestic core of the film's compact, walkable Montmartre. Amélie (2001), co-written by Guillaume Laurant and Jean-Pierre Jeunet, follows a solitary waitress who becomes an anonymous benefactor, and occasionally an anonymous avenger, in her neighbourhood. The grocery subplot is also the film's most explicit treatment of class and humiliation: the shopkeeper's contempt for his assistant, and the assistant's eventual dignity, are the moral axis around which Amélie's mischief turns.

The Collignon sequence is narratively important because it complicates the film's sweetness. Amélie answers Collignon's cruelty by entering his flat with copied keys and altering his surroundings until he doubts his own perception. The film frames this as comic justice, yet it rests on the same covert observation and manipulation that drive her benevolent schemes elsewhere. Critics have read this ambivalence as part of the film's portrait of a heroine who prefers controlling life at a distance to living it.

The location itself shows how a working business can incorporate its screen identity. The British Film Institute's anniversary comparison records that the shop is still open and now runs a crêperie named after the film, with a wall of press cuttings and a poster; the same comparison notes the rainy sequence of Amélie waiting with a polka-dot umbrella and the reverse view towards the steps at the top of the Passage des Abbesses. A “Maison Collignon” sign now hangs above the canopy, and the west-side window displays newspaper cuttings: the fictional name has been written onto the real façade.

Fan practice extends the fiction further. Visitors identify the first door on the west side of the building as the entrance to Amélie's flat, turning a private residential door into a stop on a tour. The site is therefore a compact case study in film-induced tourism: commercial adaptation, the circulation of fan knowledge, and the tension between residents' everyday use of a street and its consumption as a set.

texts.html: This is Amélie's café! In the film she works here as a waitress, serving coffee to a funny crowd of regulars. Look for the red awnings and the gold letters. Amélie is a French film from 2001 about a shy young woman who secretly makes people happy. Peek inside: the tobacco counter where Georgette sat in the film has gone.

Welcome to the Café des 2 Moulins, the most famous café in Montmartre, the hilly village in the north of Paris. In the film Amélie, this is where the heroine works as a waitress. She carries plates, listens to everyone's secrets and quietly plans how to make her customers a little happier. If you have not seen it yet: Amélie is a French film from 2001. Amélie Poulain is a shy young woman with a huge imagination who decides to help the people around her, without them knowing. The film crew shot both inside and outside the real café, so you can compare the shots with what you see today.

The café is still open. Outside, look for the red awnings and the gold letters. Inside, the dining room has hardly changed since the film. The café even serves an “Amélie” menu with crème brûlée, the dessert Amélie loves to crack with the back of a spoon. Near the toilets there is a little cabinet full of film souvenirs.

Try this: stand quietly for one minute and watch the people around you, like Amélie does. Who would you secretly help, and how?

Welcome to the Café des 2 Moulins! Its name means “café of the two windmills”, a nod to Montmartre's famous windmills, like the Moulin de la Galette up the hill and the red sails of the Moulin Rouge below. For film fans, though, this corner café belongs to one person only: Amélie Poulain. Amélie is a French film from 2001, directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet. It tells the story of a shy young woman who grew up lonely, with a big imagination, and who decides one day to make the people around her happier, in secret. You probably remember that Amélie's adventure starts in this neighbourhood on the night of 31 August 1997, when a small accident in her flat leads her to a hidden box of childhood treasures.

In the film, Amélie works here as a waitress. The café is full of funny characters: Georgette, who sells cigarettes at the counter and always thinks she is ill, and Joseph, a jealous customer who records everything on a tiny tape recorder. Amélie watches them all, and some of her secret good deeds happen right here, between the tables.

The real café is still open, and it is very proud of its film career. Outside, look for the red awnings, the gold letters and the street sign for Rue Lepic on the corner. Inside, the dining room is almost exactly as it looks on screen. There is an “Amélie” menu with crème brûlée, and a little cabinet of film memorabilia near the toilets. One thing has changed: the tobacco counter where Georgette sat is gone.

Here is a detective game for your visit. In the film, the camera often looks at the café from the street. Stand on the opposite pavement of Rue Lepic and try to find the same view: the corner, the awnings, the door. Take a photo now and compare it with the film later. What changed, and what stayed exactly the same?

Amélie loves small, secret pleasures, like dipping her hand into a sack of grain, skimming stones on a canal, or cracking the caramel top of a crème brûlée with a spoon. What are your small pleasures? Make a list of three with your group, then compare: did anybody choose the same one?

Amélie's place of work: the corner café where she waits tables among a cast of eccentric regulars. The dining room has barely changed since filming, and the café now serves an “Amélie” menu, crème brûlée included. Amélie (2001) is Jean-Pierre Jeunet's comedy about a shy Parisian who secretly arranges small happinesses for others. Only Georgette's tobacco counter is missing; the rest matches the frame closely.

On the lower slope of Rue Lepic, this corner brasserie is Amélie Poulain's workplace and the social centre of her small world. Between the coffee machine and the tobacco counter, Amélie observes the regulars, from the hypochondriac Georgette to the jealous Joseph, and quietly starts rearranging their lives for the better. Amélie, released in 2001 and directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, follows a shy young waitress in Montmartre who decides to become an anonymous do-gooder. The crew filmed both the interior and the corner front, and shots of the café recur throughout the film, which is why the place reads instantly to anyone who knows it.

The café is still trading, and it plays its role with good humour. The dining area is almost exactly as seen on screen; the menu offers an “Amélie” formula ending, of course, in crème brûlée; and a cabinet of film memorabilia hangs near the toilets. The main loss is Georgette's tobacco counter, which has been removed. Outside, red awnings and gold lettering make the corner easy to spot from Place Blanche, a short walk downhill.

Few cafés owe their fame to a single film as clearly as the Café des 2 Moulins. Before 2001 it was one of many brasseries on Rue Lepic, the winding market street that climbs from Place Blanche towards the top of the Butte Montmartre. After Amélie, it became a place of pilgrimage, and it has adapted to that role with evident pleasure. Amélie (Le Fabuleux Destin d'Amélie Poulain), directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, tells the story of a shy waitress who, after returning a box of childhood treasures to its long-lost owner, sets out to make the people around her happier without ever being seen. Jeunet and his cinematographer Bruno Delbonnel built the film's look from real Montmartre locations pushed through strong colour grading, which is why the real café looks familiar and yet slightly paler than in memory.

In the film, the café is Amélie's workplace and the stage for many small subplots. Georgette, who runs the tobacco counter, is convinced she is always ill; Joseph, a jealous former boyfriend of one of the waitresses, records every remark on a pocket tape recorder; and the regulars drift in and out with their habits and griefs. Amélie, behind the counter or among the tables, watches them all, and some of her first secret interventions happen within these walls.

The café is still trading. According to a comparison made for the film's twenty-fifth anniversary, the dining area is almost exactly as seen on screen, and the café now caters explicitly to film tourists: there is an “Amélie” menu, with crème brûlée for dessert, and a cabinet of film memorabilia near the toilets. Not everything survived, though: Georgette's tobacco counter has been removed, so the most recognisable corner of the interior is now ordinary café space.

Outside, the corner is easy to recognise: red awnings, gold letters, the word “Brasserie” and a Rue Lepic street sign on the pillar. If you stand on the opposite pavement of Rue Lepic, you will be close to the viewpoint of the exterior shots. Mornings are quieter; by lunchtime, the queue of visitors taking the same photograph is part of the scene. For the full effect, come back after dark, when the lit dining room gives the corner the warm glow of the film's interiors.

A working brasserie turned into a site of film tourism: the dining room is almost unchanged since 2001, and the café now markets itself through the film with an “Amélie” menu and a memorabilia cabinet. Film tourism means travelling to places because they appeared on screen. A clear case of a location absorbing its fictional identity.

The Café des 2 Moulins is the central social space of Jean-Pierre Jeunet's Amélie (2001): the workplace where the protagonist observes, catalogues and eventually manipulates the lives of the regulars. The interior and the corner front recur throughout the film, so the location functions less as a backdrop than as a recurring set built on a real site. In location studies, a set is a constructed space, while a location is a real place used for filming; a recurring real location can come to work like a set. Its density of character business (Georgette's counter, Joseph's tape recorder) makes the café the film's clearest microcosm of the neighbourhood community it idealises.

Twenty-five years on, the café has absorbed its fictional identity. The British Film Institute's comparison of locations notes that the dining area is almost exactly as on screen and that the café now caters explicitly to film tourists, with an “Amélie” menu and a cabinet of memorabilia. The loss of the tobacco counter, recorded by visitors, shows the opposite pressure: a working business changes, and the film image stays fixed.

The Café des 2 Moulins is the hub of Amélie's narrative geography. Jeunet's film maps a small, walkable Montmartre around three anchor points: Amélie's flat above the grocery on Rue des Trois Frères, the stations where Nino hunts discarded photographs, and this corner brasserie on Rue Lepic, where she works. The café is where the film introduces its gallery of eccentric regulars and where many of its comic subplots are staged, so it carries much of the film's social world. Amélie (2001), co-written by Guillaume Laurant and Jean-Pierre Jeunet and photographed by Bruno Delbonnel, became one of the most successful French films abroad and is widely credited with drawing visitors to Montmartre. The space is presented as a community, warm, idiosyncratic and enclosed, in which an observant outsider can intervene without being noticed.

That idealisation drew criticism when the film was released: some French critics argued that its spotless, nostalgic Montmartre left out the social and ethnic diversity of the real neighbourhood. The café is a useful place to test the argument, because it is a real, ordinary, working business whose interior the film borrowed almost unchanged and then recoloured. Built in 1801–1804, it was the first metal bridge in the city, a slender iron footbridge linking the Institut de France on the Left Bank with the Louvre, then the Palais des Arts, on the Right. Damaged over the years, it was rebuilt in the 1980s in a similar form, and it is a registered historic monument. The bar scene and the bridge form a classic pairing of enclosed and open space: emotion is first observed indoors, at a distance, then expanded outdoors, where the city itself seems to respond to the heroine's mood.

The bridge is well chosen for this function. Built in 1801–1804 as the first metal bridge in Paris, and rebuilt in the 1980s, it links the Institut de France and the Louvre, two institutions of national culture, across one of the most celebrated views of the Seine. Amélie's private epiphany is thus staged on an axis of public, monumental meaning, a characteristic blend of the intimate and the iconic that runs through the film.

The bridge's own meanings have shifted since 2001. For years it was the main site in Paris for “love locks”, padlocks attached by couples to the railings, a practice that turned it into a monument to romantic ritual until the weight of the locks threatened the structure. In 2015 the city removed them and installed glass panels over the railings. A visitor retracing Amélie's crossing therefore walks a bridge whose surface has been altered by another form of mass, image-driven tourism.

That layering is worth noting: the same structure has served as a revolutionary engineering work, a film set, a ritual site and a regulated heritage object, and each phase has left traces that visitors can read.

For a tour, the bridge is therefore an opportunity to discuss how many different publics, engineers, film-makers, couples and conservators, have successively claimed the same structure, and how each of them altered what the next would see.

Welcome to Notre-Dame de Paris, the most famous cathedral in France. People started building it in 1163, more than 850 years ago, and it took nearly two hundred years to finish. Look at the west front, facing this big square: two tall square towers, a round rose window like a giant flower made of stone and glass, and three doorways covered in carved saints, angels and kings. Can you find the gargoyles and strange creatures looking down from the towers? Amélie is a French film from 2001. It begins with Amélie's childhood: she is a lonely little girl with a strict, distant father and a nervous mother, and she spends a lot of time alone, imagining things. Did you notice that the film tells this sad moment almost like a joke? That is its style: the narrator describes even terrible events in a calm, quirky voice, like a strange fairy tale.

In the film, little Amélie comes to Notre-Dame every year with her mother to light a candle and pray for a little brother. One day, as they come out onto this square, something incredible and terrible happens: a tourist falls from the top of the cathedral and lands on Amélie's mother, who dies. It is a very sad moment, but the film tells it in such a strange, surprising way that it feels like a fairy tale. After that, Amélie grows up alone with her father, and she escapes into her imagination.

Notre-Dame has its own sad story too. On 15 April 2019 a huge fire destroyed its wooden roof and its tall spire. People all over the world watched it burn. Then hundreds of craftspeople worked for five years to rebuild it, using the same materials and techniques as in the Middle Ages, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024.

Look closely at the stone: some parts are new and very light, others are centuries old and darker. Can you spot the difference? Inside, entry is free, but there is often a queue.

Discussion: Amélie turns her sadness into imagination and, later, into kindness for others. What helps you when you feel sad?

Emily in Paris (Netflix, 2020–), created by Darren Star, follows an American marketer in Paris; French food and French chefs are central to its picture of Parisian romance. The series repeatedly frames French cuisine as authenticity, the real thing that the marketer heroine can only promote, and Gabriel's career as a struggle between craft and publicity. That an Italian restaurant performs this authenticity is a neat emblem of the show's manufactured Paris.

The location also completes the series' remarkably faithful local geography. The restaurant stands next to the Boulangerie Moderne and on the corner of Place de l'Estrapade, where Emily lives, so the fiction's compression of home, food and romance into a few steps corresponds to the real street. That faithfulness has consequences. The corner now attracts a steady flow of visitors photographing the exterior of a restaurant that serves a different cuisine from the one they associate with it. For the business, the series brings attention that is only partly convertible into custom; for visitors, the discovery that “Gabriel's restaurant” is Italian becomes part of the experience, a small lesson in how television fabricates places.

A critical visit can use the corner to discuss the difference between a location's diegetic identity, Les Deux Compères, and its everyday one, Terra Nera, and how film tourism negotiates between the two.

The case also shows how little a façade needs to do. A shop front, a terrace and a sign are enough to establish a bistro; the cuisine, the staff and the interior can all differ from the fiction without disturbing the audience. Location filming relies on this economy of signs, and film tourism, by bringing visitors to the real place, exposes it.

She hides it in a phone box, then makes the phone ring just as the man walks past, so that he finds it without ever knowing who left it there.

Amélie decides to find the owner of the box, who is now a grown man called Dominique Bretodeau. She gives the box back in secret, without telling him who she is. The use of 185 North Gower Street as 221B Baker Street in Sherlock (2010–2017) is a striking case of displacement. According to the production history of A Study in Pink, the real Baker Street was avoided because of the number of things labelled “Sherlock Holmes” there. The heritage industry built around Conan Doyle's fiction thus made its canonical address unusable for a new adaptation, which created a second, competing pilgrimage site a short distance away. Created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, the BBC series relocates Holmes and Watson to contemporary London. Fans now visit both addresses: the museum's literary 221B and the series' televisual one, a neat demonstration that the same fictional place can be anchored in different real sites by different media.

Speedy's café, appearing on screen as itself, adds a layer of everyday authenticity to the substitute.

The coexistence of the two sites, each with its own visitors, shows that location tourism does not simply follow a fiction to its source: each medium creates its own source, and fans follow the medium.

221B Baker Street is perhaps the most famous fictional address in literature, and one of the earliest objects of literary tourism: visitors have sought it since the nineteenth century, long before any number 221 existed on the street. When the BBC produced Sherlock (2010–2017), the address posed an unusual problem. According to the production history of A Study in Pink, the real Baker Street was avoided because of the number of things labelled “Sherlock Holmes” there, which would have needed disguising. Sherlock, created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, transposes Arthur Conan Doyle's detective stories to contemporary London, with Benedict Cumberbatch and Martin Freeman as Holmes and Watson. The episode is a case where the heritage industry that grew around a fiction becomes an obstacle to its renewal: the commercial landscape built to commemorate Holmes makes the canonical setting unusable for a new adaptation.

The production chose instead a Georgian terrace near Euston: the door at 185 North Gower Street, beside Speedy's Sandwich Bar & Café, became 221B and was used for exteriors throughout the series. The result is a doubled geography. The museum on Baker Street anchors the literary 221B; North Gower Street anchors the televisual one. Fans visit both, and the two sites, less than two kilometres apart, offer competing claims to the same fictional place.

Speedy's, which appears on screen as itself, contributes a particular form of authenticity: a real, unremarkable neighbourhood café, absorbed into the fiction without being disguised, whose ordinariness helps sell the modernised Holmes. The blue plaque to Giuseppe Mazzini on the neighbouring house adds a further, quite different layer of London commemoration, one of the city's many official markers of real lives, beside a fan site devoted to an invented one.

The street therefore offers a compact lesson in the layering of history, fiction and fandom that characterises literary and screen tourism in London.

For visitors, the experience is often recursive: they come to see a substitute for a fictional address, photograph it as the real thing, and then perhaps walk to Baker Street to see the museum's version, which is itself a reconstruction. Each site authenticates the fiction differently, and neither is more real than the other.

Sherlock is a British TV series that started in 2010. It brings Sherlock Holmes, the brilliant detective invented by Arthur Conan Doyle more than 130 years ago, into modern London. First, this is where the whole story begins. In the very first episode, a friend brings John Watson, just back from the army, to the hospital laboratory to meet a strange man who needs a flatmate. It is the beginning of a great friendship.

Second, this is where the most famous cliffhanger of the series happens. At the end of the second series, Sherlock's enemy Moriarty has trapped him with a cruel plan. Sherlock goes up onto the roof of Barts and phones John, who is standing in the street below. He says goodbye, and then he falls. Was it a trick? Did he survive? Fans had to wait two whole years for the next series to find out, and they invented hundreds of theories!

In Sherlock, Barts frames the central relationship of the series. Sherlock deduces John's recent past at a glance and proposes they share a flat at 221B Baker Street. Molly Hooper, the pathologist who works at Barts, becomes a recurring presence.

At the end of the second series, in “The Reichenbach Fall”, first broadcast in January 2012, the hospital returns for the climax. Moriarty has engineered a campaign to brand Sherlock a fraud. The image of the falling detective, and the question of how he survived, fuelled two years of theories before the next series offered its explanations.

Created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, the BBC series relocates Holmes and Watson to contemporary London. The two-year interval before the next series reproduced, in compressed form, the historical experience of Conan Doyle's readers, who waited a decade for Holmes's return, and generated an extensive culture of fan theorising.

St Bartholomew's Hospital occupies a structural position in Sherlock (2010–2017). It is where Holmes and Watson first meet, in A Study in Pink, when John Watson, an army doctor invalided home from Afghanistan, is introduced to Sherlock in the hospital laboratory and agrees to share a flat at 221B Baker Street. And it is where their partnership is apparently ended, in “The Reichenbach Fall” (2012), when Sherlock, discredited by Moriarty, phones John from the roof and falls. The episode's handling of geography is instructive: the hospital roof is a real London location, while scenes set at the Tower of London were filmed at Cardiff Castle, a reminder that the series' London is a composite of real sites, substitutes and studio sets.

The fall adapts Conan Doyle's “The Final Problem” (1893), in which Holmes grapples with Professor Moriarty at the Reichenbach Falls in Switzerland and is presumed dead. The series replaces the sublime Alpine landscape with the urban vertigo of a hospital roof, and the physical struggle with a scheme to destroy Sherlock's reputation, which makes the climax as much about public image and media credibility as about violence, fitting the series' interest in a celebrity detective.

The adaptation also reproduced the reception history of the original. Conan Doyle's readers waited a decade for Holmes's return; viewers of Sherlock waited two years, a period filled with intense online speculation about how the fall was staged. Barts became a site of that participatory culture, where fans gathered to look at the roof and imagine solutions, and the hospital's façade, with its carved name, became an emblem of the series.

As a location, Barts thus layers a medical institution of nearly nine centuries with a fan memory of barely more than a decade, both legible on the same façade.

The first meeting is itself a homage. In A Study in Scarlet (1887), Conan Doyle's first Holmes story, Holmes and Watson are introduced in a chemical laboratory at Barts, and the series keeps that setting while updating everything around it: the army doctor back from Afghanistan, the search for affordable lodgings, the flat at 221B. The solution is one of the series' neatest jokes about London. The great detective's breakthrough comes from the most ordinary object in the city, a fitting twist for a series that delights in hiding the extraordinary in the everyday.

“The Blind Banker” (2010), the second episode of Sherlock, adapts Conan Doyle's “The Adventure of the Dancing Men”, replacing its stick-figure cipher with symbols painted across London and solved, as a book cipher, through the London A–Z. The episode thus inherits not only Conan Doyle's plots but also the late-Victorian imaginary of the foreign criminal underworld that runs through much detective fiction of the period.

The real Gerrard Street complicates that image. Since the decades after the Second World War, when Chinese businesses moved into Soho, it has been a commercial and community centre, now pedestrianised and decorated with lanterns and gates, and a major site of public celebrations such as Chinese New Year. Visiting with the episode in mind invites a comparison between the screen's genre conventions and the everyday life of a neighbourhood.

For a critical tour, the street is therefore a useful stop to discuss how adaptations negotiate the problematic inheritances of their source texts, and what responsibilities a location carries when it is used to stand for a community.

The episode's reception confirms the point.
