texts.html: Wow, look at all the colours! Every wall here is covered in graffiti. In Sherlock, a street artist called Raz helps Sherlock and John find secret symbols painted on these walls. Sherlock is a BBC series about a modern Sherlock Holmes. The graffiti changes all the time, so it never looks the same twice!

Under the big concrete buildings of the Southbank Centre, by the river, there is a space where every pillar and every wall is covered in graffiti, and where skateboarders and BMX riders do tricks all day long. It is one of the most famous skate spots in the world. In the Sherlock episode “The Blind Banker”, Sherlock and John come here to meet Raz, a graffiti artist Sherlock knows. Raz knows the painted walls of London better than anyone, and he helps them find more of the mysterious symbols they are investigating. Sherlock is a British TV series that started in 2010. It brings Sherlock Holmes, the great detective invented by Arthur Conan Doyle, into modern London, where he solves mysteries with his friend John Watson. Notice how the graffiti changes: artists paint over each other all the time, so the walls you see today are completely different from the ones in the episode.

Stay at the edge and watch: the skaters move fast. Which piece of graffiti would you choose as a secret symbol?

The space was built in 1967 as a walkway, and skaters discovered it in 1973. That is more than fifty years of skating in the very same spot!

Welcome to the Undercroft, the space underneath the Queen Elizabeth Hall, part of the Southbank Centre, a group of big concrete concert halls and galleries by the river. Skateboarders have been coming here for decades, and every pillar, wall and ceiling is covered in layers and layers of graffiti. Some people think it is messy; many others think it is one of the most exciting places in London. It is such a famous skate spot that people campaigned to save it when there were plans to move it. Sherlock is a British TV series that started in 2010. It brings Sherlock Holmes, the brilliant detective invented by Arthur Conan Doyle, into modern London. Sherlock solves mysteries with his friend Dr John Watson. Detective detail: in the original Sherlock Holmes story behind this episode, “The Adventure of the Dancing Men”, the secret code was made of tiny drawings of dancing figures. In the TV version, the code is painted on walls, like graffiti.

In the Sherlock episode “The Blind Banker”, strange symbols are appearing painted on walls around London, and Sherlock and John need to understand them. So Sherlock brings John here to meet Raz, a graffiti artist he knows. Raz knows every painted wall in the city, and he helps them read the graffiti. Together they find more of the mysterious symbols, although at first nobody can work out what they mean.

Look carefully at the walls today. Graffiti artists paint over each other's work all the time, so the walls you see are completely different from the ones in the episode, and they will be different again next month. Only the concrete pillars and the shape of the space stay the same.

Safety first: the skaters and BMX riders move fast, so stay at the edge and never walk across the skating area.

Art challenge: design your own tag, a signature in graffiti style, on a piece of paper. What shape and colours would show who you are?

Here is a surprising fact: the undercroft was never designed for skateboarding. It opened in 1967 as a covered walkway, and in 1973 skaters discovered that its slopes and steps were perfect for tricks. Today it is shared by skateboarders, BMX riders, graffiti artists and photographers, which makes it one of the liveliest corners of the whole river bank.

The graffiti-covered undercroft where, in “The Blind Banker”, the street artist Raz helps Sherlock and John read the city's walls and find more of the mysterious cipher symbols. Sherlock (2010–2017) modernises Conan Doyle's detective. The paint changes constantly; the pillars do not.

Beneath the Queen Elizabeth Hall, by the river between Hungerford and Waterloo bridges, the Southbank Centre's undercroft has been a skateboarding space for decades, its concrete pillars and walls covered in ever-changing layers of graffiti. In “The Blind Banker”, the second episode of Sherlock, Sherlock brings John here to meet Raz, a graffiti artist who helps them read the city's painted surfaces. They find more of the symbols at the heart of the case, though at first they cannot decode them. Sherlock (2010–2017), created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, stars Benedict Cumberbatch and Martin Freeman as a contemporary Holmes and Watson. The location suits the episode's update of Conan Doyle's “Dancing Men”: a code once scribbled on garden walls becomes a language of urban graffiti, and Sherlock's network of informants extends to the city's street artists.

The space belongs to its skaters, so watch from the edge. Chinatown, the episode's other main location, is fifteen minutes' walk north across the Golden Jubilee Bridges.

Opened in 1967 as a pedestrian walkway, the undercroft was adopted by skaters in 1973: a found space rather than a purpose-built skatepark, which is precisely what its users value.

The Southbank Centre, the cluster of concrete concert halls and galleries built on the South Bank from the 1950s to the 1960s, is one of London's great examples of post-war modernist architecture, admired and disliked in equal measure. Beneath the Queen Elizabeth Hall, its riverside undercroft became a skateboarding space in the 1970s and has remained one ever since, its pillars and walls covered in constantly renewed graffiti. When redevelopment plans threatened it in the 2010s, a vigorous campaign by skaters and supporters kept it open. Sherlock (2010–2017), created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat for the BBC, transposes Arthur Conan Doyle's detective stories to contemporary London, with Benedict Cumberbatch as Holmes and Martin Freeman as Watson. The scene illustrates one of the series' signature updates: Conan Doyle's Holmes relied on the Baker Street Irregulars, a gang of street children; the modern Sherlock relies on a network of the city's marginal experts, here a graffiti artist who can read its walls.

In “The Blind Banker”, first broadcast in August 2010, mysterious symbols painted across London are linked to a series of deaths. Sherlock brings John to the undercroft to meet Raz, a graffiti artist he knows, who helps them read the painted walls. They find more of the symbols, though at first nobody can decipher them; the solution, a book cipher keyed to the London A–Z, comes later in the episode.

The location is a natural fit for an episode that turns Conan Doyle's “Dancing Men” cipher into a language of urban marks. It also captures something of the series' London: not only the heritage city of Baker Street and Barts, but also the concrete, layered, contested spaces of the contemporary city.

Today's graffiti will not match the episode, since the walls are repainted constantly; look instead at the pillars and the shape of the space. The skaters have priority, so watch from the riverside edge. The Queen's Walk leads east to Gabriel's Wharf and west to the London Eye and the Aquarium.

The undercroft was never designed for skating. It opened in 1967 as a pedestrian walkway beneath the Queen Elizabeth Hall's foyer, and skaters discovered in 1973 that its banks and steps suited their tricks. The Long Live Southbank campaign that defended it won the support of the Mayor of London in 2014, the redevelopment plans were suspended, and the space was later refurbished for its users.

A contested modernist undercroft, home to skaters and graffiti, where “The Blind Banker” turns Conan Doyle's dancing-men cipher into urban writing read by a street artist. The scene is from series 1, episode 2. The palimpsest city as a source of clues.

In “The Blind Banker” (2010), the undercroft of the Southbank Centre, a skateboarding space since the 1970s, covered in constantly overwritten graffiti, becomes the place where Sherlock and John, guided by the graffiti artist Raz, read the city's walls for the symbols at the centre of the case. The episode thus recasts Conan Doyle's cipher of “The Dancing Men” as urban writing, and the city as a palimpsest of signs requiring expert interpreters. A palimpsest is a surface written over many times, with traces of earlier layers still visible. The choice of a space later defended by a high-profile campaign against redevelopment also inscribes the series in debates about who owns and shapes public space in regenerated London.

Because the graffiti is constantly repainted, the location's architecture, not its surface, is what remains identifiable.

Opened in 1967 as a pedestrian walkway and appropriated by skaters from 1973, it is a found space rather than a designed skatepark: its meaning was produced by its users, not by its architects.

The undercroft of the Southbank Centre, beneath the Queen Elizabeth Hall, has been occupied by skateboarders since the 1970s. Its walls and pillars carry layer upon layer of graffiti, painted over continually, so that the space is never visually the same for long. In the 2010s, a proposal to replace it with retail units was met by a sustained campaign by skaters and supporters, and the undercroft was preserved, making it one of the most visible cases of contested public space in contemporary London. Sherlock (2010–2017), created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, transposes Conan Doyle's stories to contemporary London; “The Blind Banker” adapts “The Adventure of the Dancing Men”. The episode's reliance on a graffiti artist as informant updates Conan Doyle's Baker Street Irregulars, the street children whose knowledge of the city Holmes employs, into a contemporary figure of urban expertise outside official institutions.

In “The Blind Banker”, Sherlock and John come here to consult Raz, a graffiti artist who helps them read the walls and find more of the mysterious symbols linked to the case. The location transforms Conan Doyle's cipher, originally a series of stick figures chalked or scribbled near a country house, into a language of urban marks, and figures the city as a palimpsest of signs requiring specialised readers. Sherlock's genius consists in reading London; here, he must borrow the literacy of a street artist.

The site's own history complicates the screen image. The graffiti seen in the episode has long since been painted over, so visitors cannot find the frame; they can find only the architecture, the pillars and the space, beneath a surface that changes month by month. The undercroft thus exemplifies a location whose identity lies in a practice rather than an image, and whose survival depended on its users' collective defence.

For a critical itinerary, the stop invites reflection on the difference between heritage preserved as an image and culture preserved as a living use.

The undercroft was not designed for skating: opened in 1967 as a pedestrian walkway beneath the foyer of the Queen Elizabeth Hall, it was first used by skateboarders in 1973. Its users still regard it as a street spot rather than a skatepark, a found space whose character depends on appropriation rather than design, which is precisely what the Long Live Southbank campaign defended.

locations.name: Sea Life London Aquarium (County Hall)
locations.identify: The huge stone County Hall, right next to the London Eye and facing the Houses of Parliament across the river. The aquarium is in its basement; look for the Sea Life signs.

heritage.status: Grade II* listed building (the main block of County Hall)

access.setting: visitor attraction in the basement of County Hall
access.notes: The scene was filmed inside the aquarium, which needs a ticket. The riverside walk outside is free and faces Parliament.

facts.text: In “The Six Thatchers”, Sherlock meets Lady Smallwood's assistant Vivian Norbury in the London Aquarium, where she confesses that she tipped off the hostage-takers in Georgia and so betrayed Mary's team.
When John, Mycroft and the police arrive, Vivian shoots at Sherlock, but Mary jumps in the way, taking the bullet; she professes her love and gratitude to John and Sherlock and dies.
“The Six Thatchers”, the first episode of series 4, was first broadcast on 1 January 2017; series 4 was primarily filmed at Pinewood Studio Wales.
The episode is loosely based on “The Adventure of the Six Napoleons”; the black pearl of the Borgias appears as a case Sherlock had dismissed.

The aquarium scenes were filmed in a single day; the aquarium's sharks have to be in bed by 2 a.m., which made filming there difficult, and cast and crew amused themselves by inventing shark facts such as “sharks like beans”.
Producer Sue Vertue: “One of the things we did find hard was the aquarium … we realised that sharks sleep at night.” Some scenes look as though they are set against a video screen of fish swimming.
Mark Gatiss on the plan for Mary's death: “It was always going to be saving Sherlock.”
Sea Life London Aquarium opened in 1997 in County Hall on the South Bank; it has been part of the Sea Life chain since 2009 and is operated by Merlin Entertainments.

County Hall, designed by Ralph Knott, was begun in 1911 and opened by King George V in 1922 as the headquarters of the London County Council, later the Greater London Council; it lost that role when Margaret Thatcher's government abolished the GLC in 1986. It is Grade II* listed, and the aquarium is in its basement.
The main block of County Hall is listed at Grade II* in the National Heritage List for England (entry 1358192, first listed in 1951).

texts.html: Sharks and thousands of other sea creatures live here, in the basement of the huge County Hall building. In Sherlock, a sad and exciting scene happens among the tanks, and the film crew had a problem: the sharks needed their sleep! Sherlock is a BBC series about a modern Sherlock Holmes. The episode is “The Six Thatchers”, from 2017.

This aquarium is hidden in the basement of County Hall, the grand stone building next to the London Eye that was once the home of London's government. Today it is full of sharks, jellyfish and thousands of other sea creatures. In the Sherlock episode “The Six Thatchers”, Sherlock follows a mystery all the way here and meets a quiet woman called Vivian Norbury among the tanks. What happens next is one of the saddest moments of the whole series: John's wife, Mary, bravely jumps in to protect Sherlock, and she does not survive. Sherlock is a British TV series that started in 2010. It brings Sherlock Holmes, the great detective invented by Arthur Conan Doyle, into modern London, where he solves crimes with his friend Dr John Watson. Behind the scenes, filming was tricky: the whole aquarium scene was shot in a single day, and the crew discovered that sharks sleep at night. The aquarium's sharks have to be in bed by 2 a.m.!

If you visit inside, look for the big shark tanks and imagine the camera crew at work in the blue light, surrounded by water. Can you find a spot that looks like the scene? Mary is a hero in this story: what makes someone brave, in your opinion?

Welcome to County Hall! This enormous stone building beside the London Eye was opened in 1922 by King George V, and for more than sixty years it was the home of London's government. Today it is full of attractions, and down in its basement is the Sea Life London Aquarium, home to sharks, jellyfish and thousands of other sea creatures. Sherlock is a British TV series that started in 2010. It brings Sherlock Holmes, the great detective invented by Arthur Conan Doyle, into modern London, where he solves crimes with his friend Dr John Watson. A strange coincidence for detectives: “The Six Thatchers” is about smashed statues of Margaret Thatcher, and its saddest scene was filmed in the building whose London council her government abolished in 1986!

In the Sherlock episode “The Six Thatchers”, from 2017, someone is smashing little statues, called busts, of Margaret Thatcher, a famous British prime minister. Sherlock wants to know why. The trail leads him to a hidden secret about John's wife, Mary, who used to be a secret agent, and finally to this aquarium, where he meets a quiet woman called Vivian Norbury among the tanks.

This is where one of the saddest scenes of the whole series takes place. Vivian points a gun at Sherlock, but Mary bravely jumps in the way to protect him. She is hit, and she does not survive. Before she dies, she tells John and Sherlock how much she loves them. It is a scene about friendship and courage, and it changes everything for John and Sherlock.

Making the scene was tricky. The whole aquarium sequence was filmed in a single day, and the crew found out that sharks sleep at night: the aquarium's sharks have to be in bed by 2 a.m.! To keep themselves amused during filming, the actors and crew made up silly shark facts, like “sharks like beans” and “sharks cannot spell”.

Visiting tip: the aquarium needs a ticket. If you go in, look for the big shark tanks and see whether you can find a spot that looks like the scene. Outside, the riverside walk has one of the best views in London, straight across the Thames to the Houses of Parliament.

County Hall, the vast stone building beside Westminster Bridge, was designed by Ralph Knott, begun in 1911 and opened by King George V in 1922 as the headquarters of the London County Council. It later housed the Greater London Council, until Margaret Thatcher's government abolished the GLC in 1986 and the building lost its role as the seat of London's government. Now a Grade II* listed building given over to hotels and attractions, it has the Sea Life London Aquarium, opened in 1997, in its basement. Sherlock (2010–2017), created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat for the BBC, transposes Arthur Conan Doyle's detective to contemporary London, with Benedict Cumberbatch as Sherlock Holmes and Martin Freeman as John Watson. The location adds an irony worth noticing: a story built around smashed busts of Margaret Thatcher reaches its climax in the building whose council her government abolished.

“The Six Thatchers”, first broadcast on 1 January 2017, opens Sherlock's fourth series. A string of smashed busts of Margaret Thatcher leads Sherlock to a memory stick hidden inside one of them, and to Mary Watson's past as a freelance agent in a team called AGRA, betrayed during a hostage rescue in Tbilisi. The trail ends at the aquarium, where Lady Smallwood's assistant, Vivian Norbury, confesses that she was the traitor.

When John, Mycroft and the police arrive, Vivian fires at Sherlock, and Mary throws herself into the bullet's path. She dies after telling John and Sherlock how much she loves them, and John, grief-stricken, blames Sherlock, who had vowed to protect her. Mark Gatiss later explained that Mary's death “was always going to be saving Sherlock”.

Like most of the fourth series, the episode was made largely at Pinewood Studio Wales, but the aquarium scenes were shot here, in a single day. Filming ran into an unexpected constraint: as the producer Sue Vertue put it, the team “realised that sharks sleep at night”, and the aquarium's sharks have to be in bed by 2 a.m. Some shots look as if they were staged against a video screen of swimming fish.

The aquarium needs a ticket, and the tanks used are not documented, so treat a visit as a chance to feel the scene's enclosed, blue-lit atmosphere rather than to match a frame. Outside, the riverside walk in front of County Hall looks straight across the Thames to the Houses of Parliament.

A former seat of London government, now a leisure attraction, stages Mary Watson's death in “The Six Thatchers” (2017): an artificial sea as the setting for sacrifice, ending the Holmes–Watson household's brief domesticity. Sherlock (2010–2017) modernises Conan Doyle. The setting adds an irony to an episode about Thatcher busts.

“The Six Thatchers” (2017), which opens the fourth series of Sherlock, reaches its climax in the Sea Life London Aquarium, in the basement of County Hall, where Mary Watson takes a bullet meant for Sherlock. The setting is doubly displaced: an artificial sea installed in the former seat of London's government, a role the building lost when Margaret Thatcher's government abolished the Greater London Council in 1986. That an episode structured around smashed busts of Thatcher should end there is an irony worth noting, whether or not it was intended. Created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, Sherlock transposes Conan Doyle's stories to contemporary London; this episode loosely adapts “The Adventure of the Six Napoleons”. The death also revises the canon, in which Mary Morstan dies offstage between stories: the series converts an unexplained absence into a staged sacrifice, which Gatiss described as always having been about saving Sherlock.

Production accounts add that the scenes were shot in a single day and constrained by the sharks' sleep: the aquarium's spectacle had to be negotiated with its living inhabitants, whose rhythms set the shooting schedule.

For visitors, the site rewards attention to layering: civic architecture, a commercial attraction and a fictional death occupy the same address.

“The Six Thatchers”, first broadcast on 1 January 2017, opens the fourth series of Sherlock and loosely adapts Conan Doyle's “The Adventure of the Six Napoleons”, replacing the busts of Napoleon with busts of Margaret Thatcher. The smashed busts lead not to a jewel, as in the original, but to a memory stick and to Mary Watson's past as a freelance agent, so that the canonical puzzle becomes the vehicle for a story about the Watsons' marriage and its buried history. Sherlock (2010–2017), created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, adapts Conan Doyle's stories to contemporary London, with Benedict Cumberbatch and Martin Freeman as Holmes and Watson. The black pearl of the Borgias, the prize of the original story, survives in the episode as a case that Sherlock had earlier dismissed as uninteresting, an example of the series' habit of citing the canon in order to swerve away from it.

The climax takes place in the Sea Life London Aquarium, in the basement of County Hall. The building, opened in 1922 as the headquarters of the London County Council, lost its role as the seat of London's government when Margaret Thatcher's government abolished the Greater London Council in 1986, and has since been given over to hotels and attractions. An episode organised around smashed images of Thatcher thus ends inside the former headquarters of an institution her government dismantled, now repurposed as commercial leisure.

In the aquarium, Lady Smallwood's assistant Vivian Norbury confesses to the betrayal that destroyed Mary's team, and when she fires at Sherlock, Mary takes the bullet and dies. The scene departs from the canon, in which Mary Morstan's death occurs offstage and is mentioned only in passing; the series converts an absence into an onscreen sacrifice, which Mark Gatiss described as always having been about saving Sherlock.

The production history is also revealing. Den of Geek reported that the scenes were shot in a single day and that the schedule was shaped by the sharks, which must sleep by 2 a.m., while some shots appear to rely on a video screen of swimming fish. The aquarium's artificial sea may thus have been partly simulated in turn, a fitting layer of artifice for a location already twice removed from its original purpose.

For a critical itinerary, the stop shows how a single address can hold civic history, commercial leisure and fictional grief at once.

texts.html: On a bench by the river here, Sam tells his stepdad Daniel a big secret: he is in love with a girl at school, and it feels like total agony! Daniel is so relieved that it is only love. Love Actually is a 2003 Christmas film with many love stories. Sam later learns the drums to impress her.

This riverside walk, the Queen's Walk, runs along the south bank of the Thames, with views of St Paul's Cathedral and the City across the water. In Love Actually, Daniel is worried about his stepson Sam. Sam's mum has died, and since then he has been sad and shut away in his room. Daniel thinks Sam is grieving, but on a bench right here, Sam finally tells him the real reason: he is in love with a girl at his school, and it is total agony! Daniel is so relieved that he laughs, and promises to help. Love Actually is a British Christmas film from 2003, written and directed by Richard Curtis. It tells many love stories, all happening in London before Christmas. The girl is Joanna, the coolest girl in school, and Sam decides to learn the drums to play at the school Christmas concert, where she will be singing.

Sit down on a bench and look at the river. If you had a big secret to share with a grown-up, where would be a good place to talk?

Welcome to the Queen's Walk, the long riverside path of the South Bank. From here you can see the River Thames, the boats, the bridges and, on the other side, the great dome of St Paul's Cathedral. Behind you is Gabriel's Wharf, a little courtyard of shops and cafés painted in bright colours. Somewhere along this stretch is one of the most touching benches in any film. Love Actually is a British film from 2003, written and directed by Richard Curtis. It tells many short love stories, all connected, that happen in London in the five weeks before Christmas. Did you notice how the film shows grief and love together? Daniel is still mourning his wife, and helping Sam with his first love is what helps Daniel to smile again.

In the film, Daniel's wife, Sam's mum, has just died. Sam has been very quiet since then, spending all his time in his room, and Daniel is worried sick: he thinks Sam is overwhelmed by grief. So he takes Sam for a walk by the river, and they sit on a bench here. Finally, Sam tells him the truth. Yes, he misses his mum, but there is something else, something worse: he is in love! With Joanna, the coolest girl at his school, who does not even know he exists. For Sam, it is total agony.

Daniel is so relieved that it is only love that he almost laughs. Then he promises to help. From that moment, the two of them become a team. Sam decides to learn the drums so he can play at the school Christmas concert where Joanna will sing, and later he even runs through an airport to say goodbye to her!

Harry gets more and more desperate, and Rufus gets slower and slower.

Rufus is played by Rowan Atkinson, the actor famous for playing Mr Bean. The whole scene is a masterclass in comic timing: almost nothing happens, very slowly, and that is what makes it so funny.

Love Actually, written and directed by Richard Curtis, interweaves about ten love stories in London in the weeks before Christmas; gifts and the rituals of the season are central to most of them. The film's Christmas is resolutely commercial: presents, shopping and department stores organise its emotional economy, and the circulation of gifts maps the circulation of affection, fidelity and betrayal among its characters.

Harry, a married executive drifting into an affair with his secretary, Mia, enters the store to buy her an expensive necklace and needs speed and invisibility. The sales assistant, Rufus, offers instead an excess of service: layer upon layer of wrapping and garnish, applied with liturgical slowness. The comedy lies in the inversion of retail pleasure into an obstacle, and in Rowan Atkinson's near-silent performance of meticulous ritual against Alan Rickman's mounting panic.

The scene's afterlife within the plot is far darker. The necklace becomes the device through which Harry's wife, Karen, discovers his infidelity: finding it in his coat, she assumes it is her present, and on Christmas Day receives a different gift. Emma Thompson's response, a silent moment alone in the bedroom, gives the film its most serious passage, so that a comic set piece in a department store ultimately carries the weight of a marriage's breakdown.

As a location, Selfridges is a landmark in its own right, Grade II* listed and still central to the West End's seasonal spectacle, and the film's scene is only one of the images that draw visitors to it.

Read alongside the film's other West End locations, Grosvenor Chapel nearby and the mews of Notting Hill, the store completes a map of affluent London in which romance is enacted through rituals of consumption and ceremony. The department store is the most explicit of these: it is where love becomes a purchase, and where the purchase becomes evidence.

A mews is a little street that, long ago, was full of stables and rooms for horses and carriages, behind the big houses on the main streets. Today the old stables have become small, pretty houses, often painted in soft colours and covered with climbing plants. One of them, number 27, has one of the most famous doors in any Christmas film. In the film, it is Christmas Eve. Mark knocks on the door of number 27, where his best friend Peter lives with his new wife, Juliet. When Juliet opens the door, Mark does not say a word. He presses play on a portable stereo, and Christmas carols start to play, so that Peter, inside the house, thinks it is just carol singers. Then Mark holds up big white cards, one after the other, with messages written on them in black marker.

With his cards, Mark tells Juliet a secret: he has been in love with her all along, even though she has married his best friend. The scene's reproducibility, a few cards, a doorway and a song, explains why it is so often restaged by visitors, a form of fan performance that turns spectators into actors in a residential street.

Love Actually (2003) assembles its London from a few recurring types of place: offices, schools, airports, and the domestic interiors and doorsteps of an affluent, mostly white West London. The cue-card scene at 27 St Luke's Mews, Notting Hill, belongs to the last category. On Christmas Eve, Mark silently declares his love to Juliet, the new wife of his best friend Peter, using hand-lettered cards while carols play from a portable stereo to make Peter believe that carol singers are at the door. Written and directed by Richard Curtis, Love Actually interweaves about ten love stories in the five weeks before Christmas; it is often grouped with Curtis's Notting Hill and Four Weddings and a Funeral as a defining vision of romantic London. Critics have described the film's city as a selective, comfortable London, sometimes called Curtisland, in which wealth, whiteness and picturesque domesticity frame the romance; the pastel mews is a near-perfect emblem of that imagery.

Formally, the scene is theatrical: the doorway frames a static stage, text replaces dialogue, and diegetic music both scores the moment and conceals it. Its economy, a single set-up, a few cards and a tune, made it eminently reproducible, and it has been widely quoted and parodied in advertising, television and even reunions of the cast.

Its reception has shifted markedly. Long celebrated as the purest gesture of romantic devotion in the film, the scene is now frequently reread as an uncomfortable transgression: a man declaring himself to his best friend's wife on her doorstep, with her husband inside. The change exemplifies a broader reassessment of romantic comedy's conventions of persistence and grand gesture.

As a site of film tourism, the mews illustrates the tension between fandom and residents. Each December the doorstep attracts visitors restaging the scene with their own cards, in a private street not designed for crowds. For a critical tour, the location offers a compact case of how an image of romantic London is reproduced, contested and lived with by the people who actually live behind the door.

The scene's minimal means, a doorway, a few cards and a song, make it unusually easy to re-enact, which helps explain why it generates more fan performance than the film's spectacle-heavy scenes.

The doorstep has become a stage.

facts.text: Vauxhall Bridge is a Grade II* listed steel and granite deck arch bridge crossing the Thames between Pimlico on the north bank and Vauxhall on the south; it was listed in 2008.

The present bridge took eight years to build and opened on 26 May 1906, five years behind schedule. It replaced Regent Bridge, later renamed Vauxhall Bridge, built between 1809 and 1816: the first iron bridge over the Thames.
The first bridge was built by a private company and run as a toll bridge until it was taken into public ownership in 1879.

Eight bronze statues, installed in late 1907, stand above the piers: Frederick Pomeroy made Agriculture, Architecture, Engineering and Pottery (upstream), and Alfred Drury made Science, Fine Arts, Local Government and Education (downstream). George Frampton, first appointed with them, withdrew. Each statue weighs about two tons.
The statues are little noticed, because they cannot be seen from the bridge itself, only from the river banks or from passing boats.
It was the first bridge in central London to carry trams, horse-drawn and then electric, until tram services ended in 1951; in 1968 it and Park Lane became the first roads in London with bus lanes.
Pomeroy also made the gilt bronze Lady Justice on the dome of the Old Bailey (1905–1906).

The SIS Building at Vauxhall Cross has been the headquarters of the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) since 1994. Designed by Terry Farrell, it was completed in April 1994 and opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 14 July 1994.
Farrell's design drew on 1930s industrial modernism, such as Bankside and Battersea power stations, and on Mayan and Aztec temples.
The building has featured in James Bond films since GoldenEye (1995), and is shown under attack in The World Is Not Enough (1999), Skyfall (2012) and Spectre (2015).
For Skyfall, a model of the building 15 metres high was built at Pinewood Studios, and a special premiere was held at Vauxhall Cross for MI6 staff, who cheered when their headquarters was attacked.
In “The Six Thatchers”, Benedict Cumberbatch was filmed on Vauxhall Bridge running towards the SIS Building.
Vauxhall Bridge is Wikidata Q1142134.
It is recorded in the National Heritage List for England (entries 1393011 and 1393012), at Grade II*.

facts.text: Trinity Church Square, formerly known as Trinity Square, is a garden square in Newington, in the London Borough of Southwark.
The church in the centre of the square was built in 1824 and served as the parish church of Holy Trinity from 1826 to 1968.

Declared redundant in 1968, it was converted in 1975 into Henry Wood Hall, which has been a rehearsal and recording venue for classical music for nearly fifty years; the church's high altar is now at St Agatha's, Landport.

The statue of a king on the stone plinth in the square is Grade II listed. It was thought to be one of eight medieval statues from the north towers of Westminster Hall (late fourteenth century), or one of a pair representing Alfred the Great and Edward, the Black Prince, made for the garden of Carlton House in the eighteenth century.
Analysis in 2021 showed that the statue's upper part is Coade stone, while its legs are Roman and made of Bath stone.

The architect John Belcher, born nearby at 3 Montague Terrace (now 8 Brockham Street) in 1841, lived at number 60 from 1849 to 1852; the publisher William Tegg lived at number 11 from 1848 to 1852, and the Congregationalist minister Thomas Binney at number 40 in 1831–1832.
In “The Six Thatchers”, the scenes with the bloodhound were filmed at Borough Market and in Trinity Church Square.
Toby, the dog Sherlock borrows, is a reference to The Sign of the Four, in which a trained scent hound helps track Holmes and Watson to a boat landing.
The square is Wikidata Q18748741; Henry Wood Hall (Q26665755) was designed by Francis Octavius Bedford.

Can you find the stone king? Sherlock is a BBC series about a modern Sherlock Holmes. Toby comes from a Sherlock Holmes novel, The Sign of the Four.

Welcome to Trinity Church Square, a quiet garden square in Southwark. In “The Six Thatchers”, Sherlock and John borrow Toby, a bloodhound, to follow a scent through London, and the bloodhound scenes were filmed here and at Borough Market, just to the north. Toby is not a new idea: in the old Sherlock Holmes story The Sign of the Four, a scent hound helps Holmes and Watson follow a trail all the way to a boat landing. Now look around the square. The building in the middle was built as a church in 1824. Today it is Henry Wood Hall, where orchestras rehearse and record music. Then find the stone king on his plinth. For years nobody was sure who he was. In 2021 experts found that his top half is made of a kind of artificial stone, and his legs are Roman! Can you sniff out any other clues? Sherlock is a BBC series about a modern Sherlock Holmes and his friend, Dr John Watson. The church's old high altar is now in a church in Portsmouth, at Landport.

Welcome to Trinity Church Square! It is a garden square in Southwark, with long rows of houses all around and a big old church in the middle. It used to be called Trinity Square. Sherlock is a BBC series in which the detective Sherlock Holmes and his friend Dr John Watson solve mysteries in today's London.

In “The Six Thatchers”, Sherlock and John borrow a bloodhound called Toby to follow a scent through London. The scenes with the dog were filmed here and at Borough Market, about ten minutes to the north. Toby is a nod to the old Sherlock Holmes story The Sign of the Four, where a trained scent hound helps Holmes and Watson follow a trail all the way to a boat landing.

The church in the middle of the square was built in 1824, and from 1826 to 1968 it was the parish church of Holy Trinity. When it closed as a church, it was turned into Henry Wood Hall, and since 1975 orchestras have used it to rehearse and to record classical music. If you are lucky, you might hear them!

Now find the statue of a king on his stone plinth. He is a mystery worthy of Sherlock. Some people thought he was one of the medieval statues from Westminster Hall; others thought he was Alfred the Great, made for a royal garden in the 1700s. In 2021, experts studied him closely and found that his top half is made of Coade stone, a kind of artificial stone, while his legs are Roman and made of Bath stone! He is a listed statue, which means he is protected. The listing is Grade II, and the 2021 study showed that he was put together from parts of different ages.

Some famous people lived here too: the architect John Belcher lived at number 60 as a boy, from 1849 to 1852. Other neighbours have included the publisher William Tegg, at number 11, and the minister Thomas Binney, at number 40. Challenge: be a bloodhound! Walk once around the square and find three clues that tell you how old it is.

Trinity Church Square, formerly Trinity Square, is a garden square in Newington, in the London Borough of Southwark. The church at its centre was built in 1824 and served as the parish church of Holy Trinity from 1826 to 1968; declared redundant, it was converted in 1975 into Henry Wood Hall, a rehearsal and recording venue for classical music. The statue of a king on its plinth is Grade II listed and long puzzled historians: it was thought to be a medieval figure from Westminster Hall, or an eighteenth-century Alfred the Great made for Carlton House. Analysis in 2021 found an upper part of Coade stone on Roman legs of Bath stone. In “The Six Thatchers”, the scenes in which Sherlock and John follow Toby, a borrowed bloodhound, were filmed here and at Borough Market. Created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, Sherlock ran on BBC One from 2010 to 2017. Toby is borrowed from The Sign of the Four, where a scent hound leads Holmes and Watson to a boat landing.

Trinity Church Square, formerly known as Trinity Square, is a garden square in Newington, in the London Borough of Southwark: long terraces of houses around a railed garden, with a former church at the centre. Sherlock, created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat, moved Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson to present-day London; it ran on BBC One from 2010 to 2017.

The church was built in 1824 and was the parish church of Holy Trinity from 1826 to 1968; its architect was Francis Octavius Bedford. Declared redundant in 1968, it was converted in 1975 into Henry Wood Hall, which has served for nearly fifty years as a rehearsal and recording venue for classical music. The church's high altar is now at St Agatha's, Landport.

The statue of a king on a stone plinth in the square is Grade II listed, and its identity has long been debated. It was thought to be one of eight medieval statues from the north towers of Westminster Hall, or one of a pair representing Alfred the Great and Edward, the Black Prince, made for the garden of Carlton House in the eighteenth century. Analysis in 2021 showed that the upper part is Coade stone, while the legs are Roman, carved in Bath stone. The result suggests a composite: a figure assembled from pieces of very different ages.

The square has had notable residents: the architect John Belcher lived at number 60 from 1849 to 1852, the Congregationalist minister Thomas Binney lived at number 40 in 1831–1832, and the bookseller and publisher William Tegg lived at number 11 from 1848 to 1852. Belcher had been born nearby in 1841, at 3 Montague Terrace, now 8 Brockham Street.

In “The Six Thatchers”, Sherlock and John borrow Toby, a bloodhound, to follow a scent; the scenes with the dog were filmed here and at Borough Market, ten minutes to the north. Toby is a nod to The Sign of the Four, in which a trained scent hound helps Holmes and Watson follow a trail to a boat landing. The exact frames are not documented, so take your time and look for the angles yourself.

A Southwark garden square around Holy Trinity (1824), since 1975 Henry Wood Hall. The bloodhound scenes of “The Six Thatchers” (2017) were filmed here and at Borough Market. Sherlock (BBC One, 2010–2017) was created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat. Toby cites The Sign of the Four's scent hound.

Trinity Church Square, in Newington, centres on Holy Trinity, built in 1824 and parish church from 1826 until its redundancy in 1968; since 1975 it has been Henry Wood Hall, a rehearsal and recording venue for classical music. Its Grade II listed statue of a king illustrates the instability of attribution: it has been read as one of the late fourteenth-century figures from Westminster Hall, or as an eighteenth-century Alfred the Great for the garden of Carlton House, and in 2021 analysis showed a Coade stone upper part on Roman legs of Bath stone, an assemblage rather than a single work. In “The Six Thatchers” (2017), the scenes in which Sherlock and John follow Toby, a borrowed bloodhound, were filmed here and at Borough Market. Sherlock (BBC One, 2010–2017) was created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat. Toby cites The Sign of the Four, in which a scent hound tracks the quarry to a boat landing.

Trinity Church Square, formerly Trinity Square, is a garden square in Newington, in the London Borough of Southwark. Its centre, Holy Trinity, was built in 1824 to designs by Francis Octavius Bedford and served as a parish church from 1826 until it was declared redundant in 1968; in 1975 it became Henry Wood Hall, for nearly fifty years a rehearsal and recording venue for classical music, while its high altar went to St Agatha's, Landport. Sherlock (BBC One, 2010–2017) was created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat.

The Grade II listed statue of a king in the square is a small case study in attribution. It was long supposed to be one of eight late fourteenth-century figures from the north towers of Westminster Hall, or one of a pair, Alfred the Great and Edward the Black Prince, made for the garden of Carlton House in the eighteenth century. Analysis in 2021 found an upper part of Coade stone, a manufactured stone, joined to Roman legs of Bath stone: an assemblage whose history is more interesting than either of the identities proposed for it. The listing protects the object as found, whatever its eventual attribution.

The square also records a professional neighbourhood: the architect John Belcher lived at number 60 from 1849 to 1852, the publisher and bookseller William Tegg at number 11 from 1848 to 1852, and the Congregationalist divine Thomas Binney at number 40 in 1831–1832. Belcher had been born nearby in 1841, at 3 Montague Terrace, now 8 Brockham Street.

In “The Six Thatchers” (2017), the scenes in which Sherlock and John follow Toby, a borrowed bloodhound, were filmed here and at Borough Market. The dog is a citation: in The Sign of the Four, a trained scent hound helps Holmes and Watson follow a trail to a boat landing. The quiet Georgian square thus serves an adaptation that transposes a canonical device into a contemporary street chase, and the exact frames remain undocumented. In this sense the square, like the statue at its centre, is an assemblage of borrowed parts.

locations.name: 23–24 Leinster Gardens
locations.identify: On a street of tall, cream-painted Victorian terraces in Bayswater, numbers 23 and 24 match their neighbours at first glance; look closer and their windows are painted dark grey and their front doors have no letter boxes.

access.notes: A quiet residential street: the neighbours are real, so please keep noise down.

facts.text: Leinster Gardens is a street in Bayswater lined with tall, ornate, mid-Victorian terraced houses, many of which are listed buildings; its southern part is named Leinster Terrace.
Numbers 23 and 24 are false houses with no rooms: façades built to match their neighbours, with column-flanked porches, balconies, sash windows and pedimented upper windows.

They were built with the steam-driven Metropolitan Railway in the 1860s, to conceal an area where the tracks are uncovered and trains could release steam; the railway company hid this from residents with frontages that blend into the prestigious terrace.
The façade is 5 feet (1.5 m) thick, with a ground-level opening of the railway behind it; it has 18 dark-grey windows and front doors with no letter boxes.
At the southern end of the street, a blue plaque on 100–101 Bayswater Road marks the home of J. M. Barrie, the author of Peter Pan.
The façade of numbers 23 and 24 was used in the Sherlock episode “His Last Vow”.

“His Last Vow” was first broadcast on 12 January 2014; it was written by Steven Moffat and directed by Nick Hurran. Some filming was in Cardiff, and part in Leinster Gardens, where houses 23 and 24 were shown to be mere façades.
After Mary shoots him and he survives, Sherlock breaks out of hospital and arranges a meeting with her; using a ruse, he exposes her secret life as an assassin to John.
Mary reveals her true identity in what Sherlock calls “the empty house”, an alleyway hidden behind what are apparently the fronts of two houses in Leinster Gardens.

Inside the “house”, Mary thinks Sherlock has tricked her by positioning a dummy of himself at the end of the alley, as in Conan Doyle's “The Adventure of the Empty House”, where a dummy fools the assassin Colonel Sebastian Moran.
Leinster Gardens is Wikidata Q3229195.

texts.html: Knock, knock... nobody's home! Numbers 23 and 24 look like ordinary houses, but they are only fronts with no rooms behind, built to hide a railway. In Sherlock they become “the empty house”. Sherlock is a BBC series about a modern Sherlock Holmes. Look closely: the windows are painted grey and the doors have no letter boxes.

Knock, knock... nobody's home! This street in Bayswater is full of tall, grand Victorian houses, but numbers 23 and 24 are fakes. They have no rooms at all: they are just fronts, a wall about one and a half metres thick, built in the 1860s to hide the steam railway underneath, where trains could let off steam. Can you spot the clues? Their 18 windows are painted dark grey, and their front doors have no letter boxes. In Sherlock, these fake houses play “the empty house” in the episode “His Last Vow”. Sherlock arranges a secret meeting there with Mary, John's wife, and behind the fronts there is only an alleyway. That is where Mary finally reveals who she really is. Imagine knocking on this door and finding nothing behind it! Sherlock is a BBC series about a modern Sherlock Holmes and his friend, Dr John Watson. In the original Holmes story about an empty house, a dummy of Holmes fools an assassin.

Knock, knock... nobody's home! Welcome to Leinster Gardens, a street in Bayswater lined with tall, fancy houses from Victorian times. Numbers 23 and 24 look just like their neighbours, with columns around their front doors, balconies and lots of windows. But they hide a secret. Sherlock is a BBC series in which the detective Sherlock Holmes and his friend Dr John Watson solve mysteries in today's London.

They are not houses at all! They have no rooms. They are only fronts, a wall about one and a half metres thick, built in the 1860s when the Metropolitan Railway was built here. Its trains were pulled by steam engines, and behind the fake fronts the tracks are open to the sky, so the trains could let out their steam. The railway company built the fronts so that the street would still look smart.

Be a detective and look for clues. The fake fronts have 18 windows, all painted dark grey, and their front doors have no letter boxes, so no post can ever arrive! At the southern end of the street, a blue plaque on 100–101 Bayswater Road marks where J. M. Barrie, the author of Peter Pan, lived. Behind the fronts, at ground level, there is an opening where the railway runs.

In Sherlock, the fake houses appear in the episode “His Last Vow”. Sherlock calls them “the empty house”. He arranges a secret meeting there with Mary, the wife of his friend John, and in the story there is only a long alleyway behind the fronts. There, Mary finally reveals who she really is. Inside, she thinks Sherlock has tricked her with a dummy of himself. That is a joke for fans: in an old Holmes story called “The Adventure of the Empty House”, a dummy of Holmes is used to fool an assassin.

Challenge: stand across the street and take a photo of the two fake houses. Then show it to someone and ask them to find the fakes. Can they spot them? Then go to the end of the street and find the blue plaque for the author of Peter Pan.

At the southern end of the street, where it becomes Leinster Terrace, a blue plaque on 100–101 Bayswater Road marks the home of J. M. Barrie, the author of Peter Pan: a real address of a famous storyteller, a few minutes' walk from two famous fakes.

Leinster Gardens is a mid-Victorian terrace of ornate, largely listed houses in which numbers 23 and 24 are façades without rooms, five feet (1.5 metres) thick, built with the steam-driven Metropolitan Railway in the 1860s to conceal an uncovered stretch where trains could vent steam. Their eighteen dark-grey windows and doors without letter boxes make them a small monument to infrastructure dressed as domesticity. “His Last Vow” (2014), written by Steven Moffat and directed by Nick Hurran, casts them as “the empty house”, the meeting place where Mary reveals her identity, and stages inside them a dummy of Sherlock: a citation of “The Adventure of the Empty House”, in which a dummy deceives Colonel Sebastian Moran. A real false front thus hosts a fictional deception. Sherlock (BBC One, 2010–2017) was created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat. Some of the episode was filmed in Cardiff; the façade was filmed here.

Leinster Gardens, in Bayswater, is a street of tall, ornate, mid-Victorian terraced houses, many of them listed; its southern section is called Leinster Terrace, and a blue plaque at 100–101 Bayswater Road, at its foot, commemorates J. M. Barrie, the author of Peter Pan. Sherlock (BBC One, 2010–2017) was created by Mark Gatiss and Steven Moffat.

Numbers 23 and 24 are false houses. Built with the steam-driven Metropolitan Railway in the 1860s, they conceal an uncovered stretch of track where trains could release steam, and the railway company dressed the gap in the frontage of a prestigious terrace: Ionic porches, balconies, sash windows and pedimented upper windows, all reproduced on a wall five feet (1.5 metres) thick. The disguise is betrayed only by eighteen dark-grey windows and doors without letter boxes. As urban history, they record how early underground engineering negotiated with the decorum of a wealthy residential street.

“His Last Vow”, written by Steven Moffat, directed by Nick Hurran and first broadcast on 12 January 2014, uses the façades as “the empty house”. After surviving Mary's shot, Sherlock arranges a meeting with her there; the episode places an alleyway behind the fronts, where Mary reveals her identity and, through Sherlock's ruse, her past as an assassin is exposed to John. Production combined Cardiff locations with this street, where the houses were shown to be mere façades. The façade's ground-level opening still shows the railway behind it.

The setting is a double citation. Inside the “house”, Mary believes that Sherlock has placed a dummy of himself at the end of the alley, recalling Conan Doyle's “The Adventure of the Empty House”, in which a dummy deceives the assassin Colonel Sebastian Moran. A genuine architectural deception thus houses a fictional one, and the episode turns a curiosity of Victorian railway engineering into a figure for a character whose respectable surface conceals another life. The empty house is thus not a studio set but a surviving piece of the city, where the illusion had already been built.
